title: The trouble with 'proper' English
summary_es: Una lingüista cuenta cómo borró su acento del norte y defiende que el inglés estándar es útil, pero que ningún dialecto es un error.
prediction_prompt: Do people in your country judge others by their accent? Is any accent considered more "correct"?

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: When I was eleven, a teacher told me, quite kindly, that I would never get anywhere talking like that.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: She meant well. She was also, as it turned out, half right, which is the uncomfortable part.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: I grew up saying "nowt" for nothing and "while" where you might say until.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: By the time I left university, I had sanded all of that down to something suitably bland.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Nobody ordered me to. Nobody needed to. You simply notice who gets listened to.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Now, as a linguist, I can tell you with complete confidence that there was nothing wrong with my grammar.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Every dialect is governed by rules. "I ain't got none" obeys rules every bit as strict as "I haven't any".

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: They are merely different rules, and the people who use them rarely own the dictionaries.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: What we call "standard" English is, historically, the dialect of a triangle of land in the south-east.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: It happened to contain the court, the printing presses and two universities.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: It prevailed, in other words, for reasons of power, not of logic.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: None of which would matter if we treated accents as we treat eye colour.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: We don't. In experiment after experiment, identical words are rated as cleverer in a prestige accent.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: The same script, read in a regional voice, is judged warmer, funnier, and noticeably less competent.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Listeners are entirely sincere about this. They believe they are assessing the argument.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: And here I must be honest about my own position, because it is not a tidy one.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: I still think children should be taught the standard form, and taught it well.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: It is the key to a great many locked doors, and refusing to hand it over helps nobody.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: What I object to is the second lesson that usually comes with it.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Namely, that the language of your kitchen table is a mistake to be corrected.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: You can add a dialect without subtracting one. Millions of people switch between them without a second thought.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: My grandmother could be scathingly formal on the telephone and gloriously broad the moment she put it down.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: She would not have called that a skill. I do. I call it being bilingual in one language.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: So the next time a voice strikes you as uneducated, I would ask you to pause.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Ask whether you are hearing a lack of thought, or merely a different postcode.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: And if you catch yourself smoothing your own vowels in a job interview, forgive yourself.

segments.speaker: kate
segments.text: Then go home and say something the way your grandmother would have. It is good for the soul.

Al final de la frase, *to* se pronuncia pleno (/tuː/), no débil.
La *t* de *listened* no suena; *to* final va pleno.

tasks.prompt: What is the speaker's main argument?

options.text: Regional dialects should replace standard English in all schools
Standard English is useful, but dialects are not errors
Accents no longer affect how people are judged

tasks.rationale_es: Hay que enseñar el estándar, pero sin enseñar que el habla de casa es un error.

tasks.prompt: How does the speaker present her own view?

options.text: As somewhat conflicted but considered
As simple, obvious and beyond any dispute
As purely scientific

tasks.rationale_es: *I must be honest about my own position, because it is not a tidy one*.

tasks.prompt: Why does she say her teacher was "half right"?

options.text: Her accent really was a social disadvantage
Her grammar really was rather poor at that age
She did fail at university

tasks.rationale_es: Su gramática era correcta, pero con ese acento la escuchaban menos.

tasks.prompt: What does "You simply notice who gets listened to" suggest?

options.text: Her teachers punished her for using dialect words
Social pressure works without anyone giving orders
She was a good listener

tasks.rationale_es: Nadie se lo ordenó: bastaba con ver a quién se hacía caso.

tasks.prompt: When she says she "sanded all of that down to something suitably bland", she means she…

options.text: forgot her childhood entirely
learnt a foreign language at university instead
smoothed away her regional features

tasks.rationale_es: Limó su manera de hablar hasta dejarla neutra.

tasks.prompt: According to the speaker, why did one dialect become "standard"?

options.text: It was more logical than the others
It was spoken where power was concentrated
It was much easier for printers to spell

tasks.rationale_es: Era el habla de la corte, las imprentas y dos universidades.

tasks.prompt: She claims non-standard dialects have no grammatical rules.
tasks.rationale_es: Dice lo contrario: todos los dialectos tienen reglas, solo que distintas.

tasks.prompt: What do the experiments she mentions reveal?

options.text: Regional speakers tend to make weaker arguments
Prestige accents are harder to understand
People rate accent while thinking they rate content

tasks.rationale_es: Las mismas palabras se valoran distinto según el acento, y quien escucha cree que juzga el argumento.

tasks.prompt: She thinks schools should stop teaching standard English.
tasks.rationale_es: Cree que hay que enseñarlo, y bien.

tasks.prompt: What is "the second lesson" she objects to?

options.text: That a child's home speech is wrong
That grammar is a boring subject for children
That spelling matters most

tasks.rationale_es: Que la lengua de tu casa es un error que hay que corregir.

tasks.prompt: Why does she describe her grandmother as "bilingual in one language"?

options.text: Because she spoke two foreign languages
Because she moved easily between two varieties
Because she had very little formal schooling as a girl

tasks.rationale_es: Pasaba del registro formal al dialecto sin esfuerzo.

tasks.prompt: What does she ask listeners to do when a voice sounds "uneducated"?

options.text: Question their own reaction
Correct the speaker politely but firmly
Ignore the accent completely

tasks.rationale_es: Pararse a pensar si oyen falta de ideas o solo otro código postal.

tasks.prompt: She condemns people who modify their accent at interviews.
tasks.rationale_es: Pide que se perdonen: ella misma lo hizo.

tasks.reference: She meant well. She was also, as it turned out, half right, which is the uncomfortable part.
tasks.rationale_es: *as it turned out* se dice muy seguido.

tasks.rationale_es: Los *to* del final de frase se pronuncian plenos.
